question: Why do we take a musculoskeletal history before doing a physical exam on a patient?

options.A: To measure the patient's exact bone density accurately
options.B: To provide context for interpreting physical findings safely
options.C: To replace the need for diagnostic blood tests entirely
options.D: To determine the exact surgical procedure required

explanation: Gathering a thorough history first gives you the background story you need to understand what you find during the physical exam. Great job! [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why must a nurse figure out if a patient's bone or joint problem is an acute injury or a long-term chronic condition?

options.A: Chronic conditions always require immediate emergency surgery
options.B: Chronic conditions cannot be assessed using standard nursing interviews
options.C: Acute injuries never involve any swelling or localized pain
options.D: Acute injuries and chronic conditions require completely different management approaches

explanation: Spot-on! Knowing whether a problem happened suddenly or built up over time completely changes how you care for and manage the patient. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h1)

question: Postmenopausal women are at a higher risk for which bone condition because their hormone levels drop?
explanation: You got it! The drop in estrogen after menopause speeds up bone loss, putting older women at high risk for osteoporosis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h2)

question: How does knowing basic biographical data like a patient's age and gender help during a bone and joint assessment?

options.A: It helps identify risk factors associated with specific demographic groups
options.B: It measures the exact strength of the patient's muscle fibers
options.C: It proves whether the patient has an active bacterial infection
options.D: It provides a definitive diagnosis without needing further tests

explanation: Exactly! Knowing age and gender helps you anticipate certain health conditions that are more common in specific groups. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h2)

question: In a patient health history, what do we mean by the 'chief complaint'?

options.A: The primary reason the patient is seeking care, in their own words
options.B: The surgical history from the patient's childhood
options.C: The final medical diagnosis written by the attending physician
options.D: A complete list of every prescription medication the patient takes

explanation: Spot-on! The chief complaint is simply the main trouble or symptom that brought the patient to the clinic, written using what they tell you. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h3)

question: Why is it important to ask if a patient's joint pain started suddenly after an accident or came on slowly?

options.A: It helps differentiate between acute traumatic injuries and chronic degenerative diseases
options.B: It measures the patient's baseline daily fluid intake
options.C: It proves whether the patient requires emergency psychological counseling
options.D: It indicates the exact blood pressure medication the patient needs

explanation: You nailed it. Sudden pain usually points to trauma like a fall, while slow pain often means wear-and-tear or arthritis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h3)

question: When assessing pain using the PQRST mnemonic, what does the letter 'Q' stand for?
explanation: Correct! 'Q' stands for quality—like asking the patient if the pain feels sharp, dull, stabbing, or aching. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h4)

question: A patient says their knee pain gets worse when climbing stairs and feels better when resting. Which part of PQRST is this?
explanation: Well done! Things that trigger pain (like stairs) are provoking factors, and things that soothe it (like rest) are palliating factors. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why should a nurse be concerned if a patient breaks a bone easily from just a minor bump or fall?

options.A: It raises suspicion for underlying bone weakness or metabolic bone disease
options.B: It confirms the patient has normal bone mineral density
options.C: It indicates that the patient has a severe muscular infection
options.D: It proves the patient engages in professional contact sports

explanation: Spot-on! Bones shouldn't break from minor bumps. This is a huge warning sign for conditions like osteoporosis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h5)

question: How does asking about a patient's family medical history help during a musculoskeletal assessment?

options.A: It replaces the need to perform a physical examination of the joints
options.B: It guarantees that the patient will develop the exact same surgical complications
options.C: It shows the exact dietary habits of the patient's household
options.D: It highlights inherited conditions like gout or osteoporosis that may affect the patient

explanation: You got it! Many bone and joint problems run in families, so knowing the family history helps you spot risks early. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h5)

question: Taking which class of medications for a long time is well-known to cause bone loss and muscle weakness?
explanation: Correct! Long-term use of corticosteroids interferes with how the body handles calcium, often leading to bone thinning. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why must nurses specifically ask patients about over-the-counter painkillers during a medication review?

options.A: Patients often do not consider non-prescription drugs as 'real' medications to report
options.B: Non-prescription drugs completely cure all forms of arthritis
options.C: Over-the-counter drugs have no side effects on bones or joints
options.D: Patients are legally prohibited from taking pain relievers at home

explanation: Spot-on! Patients often forget to mention everyday painkillers they buy over the counter, even though they can cause side effects or interact with other drugs. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h6)

question: What do Activities of Daily Living (ADLs) focus on when you are checking a patient's functional health?

options.A: Advanced athletic endurance and cardiovascular fitness
options.B: Complex financial management and household budgeting
options.C: Basic self-care tasks like bathing, dressing, and eating
options.D: Professional job performance in an office setting

explanation: You nailed it! ADLs are the everyday things we do to take care of ourselves independently, like getting dressed and eating. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h7)

question: Why is regular exercise and an active lifestyle good for a patient's bone health?

options.A: Lifestyle habits have no direct connection to skeletal strength
options.B: Weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone density and strengthens supporting muscles
options.C: Sedentary habits automatically increase vitamin D absorption in the skin
options.D: Exercise prevents all forms of genetic joint disease completely

explanation: Exactly right! Putting gentle physical stress on bones through movement tells the body to build stronger, denser bones. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h7)

question: If a patient has joint pain along with skin rashes and unusual sensitivity to sunlight, what systemic condition might they have?
explanation: Spot-on! Lupus is an autoimmune disease famous for causing joint pain alongside a butterfly-shaped face rash and sun sensitivity. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h8)

question: Why does a nurse ask about other body systems when a patient comes in with joint pain?

options.A: It proves that the joint pain is entirely psychological in origin
options.B: Systemic symptoms never occur alongside orthopedic complaints
options.C: It replaces the need to ask about the patient's current medications
options.D: Many musculoskeletal disorders are part of broader systemic or autoimmune diseases

explanation: Great job! Joint pain is often just one piece of a bigger puzzle involving the whole body, like an autoimmune condition. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T2#GNS222_U1_T2_h8)
